# Persistent Structures & Structural Sharing

In Clojure (and in React state, Git, and database snapshots) data is **never changed in place**. "Changing" it makes a new version, and the old one stays exactly as it was. That sounds expensive: surely each change copies everything?

It doesn't. A **persistent** structure copies only the **path** from the top down to the change, and **shares** everything else with the old version. The question: **how much is really shared, and what does keeping every version cost?**

How the cells run:

- **Clojure runs in your browser** (Scittle), and shares the trees by printing a `__NB_SET__` line.
- **The 3D view is an HTML cell** that keeps every version and lets you add more; **JavaScript** measures sharing over 200 inserts.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. Copy the path, share the rest

> In Clojure, build a persistent binary search tree with path copying: insert rebuilds the nodes on the path it walks and reuses the branches it doesn't. Give every node a unique id from a counter so sharing can be proved. Build tree A from 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35 and 45, then tree B by inserting 42 into A, and print how many nodes the insert made and how many B shares with A. Publish nb.pbst = {a, b}, each {root, nodes: [{id, val, left, right}]}, with a `__NB_SET__` line.

- **`insert`** never changes a node. Going down, it rebuilds each node it passes with one new child; every branch it doesn't walk down is the *same* map, reused.
- **The ids prove it.** Every `node` call takes a new id from `counter`, so a node with the same id in both trees is literally the same object.
- **Tree A is still intact** afterwards: nothing in it was touched.

(require '[clojure.string :as str])

;; Every allocated node gets a unique id - that is our proof of sharing.
(def counter (atom 0))
(defn node [v l r] {:id (swap! counter inc) :val v :left l :right r})

;; Path copying: the branch we walk is rebuilt (new ids), the branch we
;; don't walk is REUSED (same map, same id).
(defn insert [t v]
  (cond
    (nil? t)       (node v nil nil)
    (< v (:val t)) (node (:val t) (insert (:left t) v) (:right t))
    (> v (:val t)) (node (:val t) (:left t) (insert (:right t) v))
    :else          t))

(defn build [vals] (reduce insert nil vals))

(defn collect [t]
  (when t
    (concat [{:id (:id t) :val (:val t)
              :left (when (:left t) (:id (:left t)))
              :right (when (:right t) (:id (:right t)))}]
            (collect (:left t))
            (collect (:right t)))))

(def tree-a (build [50 30 70 20 40 60 80 35 45]))
(def before @counter)
(def tree-b (insert tree-a 42))
(def allocated (- @counter before))

(def ids-a (set (map :id (collect tree-a))))
(def ids-b (set (map :id (collect tree-b))))
(def shared (count (filter ids-a ids-b)))

(println "tree A:" (count ids-a) "nodes")
(println "insert 42 allocated only" allocated "new nodes (the root-to-leaf path)")
(println "tree B:" (count ids-b) "nodes," shared "of them SHARED with tree A")
(println "tree A still intact:" (count (collect tree-a)) "nodes, untouched")

(defn node-json [n]
  (format "{\"id\":%d,\"val\":%d,\"left\":%s,\"right\":%s}"
          (:id n) (:val n)
          (or (:left n) "null") (or (:right n) "null")))
(defn tree-json [t]
  (str "{\"root\":" (:id t) ",\"nodes\":["
       (str/join "," (map node-json (collect t))) "]}"))

(println (str "__NB_SET__ {\"key\":\"pbst\",\"value\":{\"a\":" (tree-json tree-a)
              ",\"b\":" (tree-json tree-b) "}}"))

- **One layer per version.** Each node sits in the layer of the version that made it. A new version is only a few nodes, a path, whose branches reach back (white lines) into older layers.
- **Slide between versions.** v0 is tree A; v1 lights A's shared nodes plus 42's path.
- **Insert your own.** Try 65, then 10, then 42 again: inserting a value that's already there still copies the path to it, because `insert` rebuilds every node it passes on the way back up.

## 3. What does keeping every version cost?

> In JavaScript, measure persistence at scale: insert 200 random numbers below 1,000 (seeded) into a path-copying tree, keeping every version. Count the nodes made in total against what a full copy per version would need, and the nodes made per insert, and print them with the final tree's size and height. Return a Vega-Lite line chart of nodes in memory against inserts for both ways, log scale.

If every version were a full copy, memory would grow with the *square* of the number of changes. With path copying, each insert costs only the depth of the tree.

## 4. Clojure's own collections

> In Clojure, show the same trick in the built-in vector: make a vector of 100,000 small maps, assoc a new map at index 50,000, time it, check the original is unchanged and the new version changed, and use identical? to show that entry 99,999 is the very same object in both but entry 50,000 is not.

The toy tree copies a path of about log2(n) nodes. Clojure's vectors and maps do the same on trees with **32 children per node**, so the path is about log32(n): 4 nodes for 100,000 entries.

- **`identical?`** asks "the very same object?", not "equal?". The untouched entry is shared; the changed one is new.

;; The built-ins do the same trick at scale: a vector is a tree with 32 children per node,
;; so changing one entry copies about 4 small nodes and shares everything else.
(def big (vec (map (fn [i] {:n i}) (range 100000))))   ; 100,000 small maps

;; A clock in nanoseconds: the JVM has one built in, the browser counts in milliseconds.
(defn now-ns [] #?(:clj (System/nanoTime) :cljs (* 1e6 (js/performance.now))))

(def t0 (now-ns))
(def big2 (assoc big 50000 {:n :changed}))
(def micros (/ (- (now-ns) t0) 1000.0))

(println (format "assoc into a 100,000-entry vector: %.1f microseconds" micros))
(println "original untouched:  " (= {:n 50000} (big 50000)))
(println "new version changed: " (= {:n :changed} (big2 50000)))
;; identical? asks "the very same object?", not "equal?".
(println "entry 99999 is the same object in both:" (identical? (big 99999) (big2 99999)))
(println "entry 50000 is not:                    " (identical? (big 50000) (big2 50000)))

## What the run shows

- **Inserting 42 makes 5 nodes and shares 5.** Tree B has 10 nodes: the copied path 50 → 30 → 40 → 45 plus the new 42, and five nodes (20, 35, 70, 60, 80 and their branches) that are the very same objects as in tree A. Tree A still has its 9 nodes, untouched.
- **In the 3D view, each insert is a thin path.** Inserting 65 then 10 gives v2 and v3; v3 has 12 nodes, but only 4 of them are new. The four versions together hold 22 nodes, where four full copies would need 42.
- **Over 200 inserts the gap is 11 times.** Keeping all 201 versions with path copying takes 1,709 nodes; a full copy of each would take 18,509. Each insert made 8.54 nodes on average, about the depth of the tree (height 16 by the end), and version 10 is still exactly as it was.
- **A value that is already there still copies its path.** `insert` returns the existing node, but every node above it is rebuilt on the way back up. The *Try this* below makes it share instead.
- **Clojure's vectors share too.** Changing one entry of a 100,000-entry vector took well under a millisecond in the browser; afterwards entry 99,999 is the same object in both versions and entry 50,000 is not.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Predict, then insert.** In the 3D view, how many new nodes will inserting 65 make? Count the path: 50, 70, 60, then 65 itself. Then press Insert.
- **Share duplicates too.** Press ✨ on the first Clojure cell and add: *"When the value is already there, return the same tree without copying anything."* Then insert 40 and count the new nodes.
- **Undo for free.** Press **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** and ask: *"In JavaScript, keep a list of versions of a to-do list made with path copying, and add undo and redo by moving along the list."*
- **Delete.** Press ✨ on the first Clojure cell and add: *"Also delete 30 from tree A by path copying, and count the nodes the delete makes."*
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the first Clojure cell and ask why tree A is still intact.
